reviewer_comments.reviewer_1:
This study analyses the concentrations and properties of magnetic minerals from the lower Eocene Contessa road section (Italy) in order to deduce the paleoenvironmental and paleoclimatic evolution of the western Mediterranean area. The manuscript confirms the results from previous studies carried out in this section and elsewhere, which showed that pelagic sedimentation in the area was astronomically forced and several short-lived (<200 ky-long) carbon-cycle perturbations occurred when long and short eccentricity maxima overlapped. Additionally, the authors found that western Mediterranean conditions became generally drier as the early Eocene climate became progressively warmer (eventually leading to the early Eocene climatic optimum), although this trend was interrupted during a ~500 ky-long wetter interval at approximately 55 Ma. They also deduce that extremely dry conditions occurred during the short-lived carbon cycle perturbations and that the recovery to pre-event conditions was fast (23-27 ky). They suggest that these results may be relevant to our understanding of the evolution and impact of anthropogenic global warming.

The manuscript is a potentially good fit for the journal and its readers. The authors have gone to great lengths with their research and show a sound understanding of the subject. However, there are some loose ends and there is room for improvement in terms of methodology and how the results are interpreted and presented.

MAJOR ISSUES
(1) It is not clear how CFB parameters were obtained. For example, was the carbonate content of each sample separated using physicochemical treatments in the laboratory (i.e., were samples decarbonated) and were the mineralogical properties of the residue subsequently analysed? Alternatively, was the carbonate content subtracted by theoretical calculations? The method used should be more clearly explained. The former method would probably also allow for the identification of clay and magnetic mineral phases by X ray diffraction, which would help to support (or refute) some of the authors’ interpretations.
(2) Why all magnetic minerals are interpreted to be detrital and why some (e.g., magnetite) are not (partly) biogenic or authigenic should also be more clearly explained. In addition, pigmentary haematite in red bed sequences is usually secondary and probably formed in the order of 105-106 years after deposition (Kodama, 2012). Could this affect the interpretation of shorter hydroclimate variations?
(3) From the very beginning (line 108) the authors state that the variations in the carbonate/clay ratio throughout the succession record variations in the rate of carbonate deposition or dissolution, later favouring dissolution as the main controlling factor (line 227). The line of reasoning should be more clearly explained. Initially, they ignore that clay (and magnetic mineral) content could also vary as a consequence of changes in the rate of terrigenous sediment input over time (i.e., terrigenous dilution). This possibility is only considered later in the manuscript, and restricted to the interpretation of the EETZ (lines 241-248). In order to address these issues further, the authors could obtain some terrigenous input proxies (e.g., Ti/Al and Zr/Al ratios) throughout the succession.
(4) PCA2all scores are used as a proxy of variations in the rates of detrital input and CaCO3 dissolution over time. However, each of the factors identified by the PCA analysis should represent only one controlling mechanism, not two (i.e., PCA2all should represent variations in either detrital input or CaCO3 dissolution, but not in both). Furthermore, both Ca (i.e., carbonates) and magnetic parameters show negative loadings in PCA2all, suggesting that they are related. Consequently, why do the authors relate negative PCA2all values only with detrital supplies in Fig. 6e? Why does Ca increase in EETZ? In addition, matrices of all PCA analyses (tables with loadings between variables and principal components) should also be provided in the supplementary material in order to know which variables are relevant to each component and their statistical significance.
(5) Regarding spectral analysis and orbital forcing, it should be emphasized that the power spectra are rather noisy and spiky (Fig. 7), meaning that there are significant periodicities that the authors seem to ignore. The original data used for the spectral analysis should be provided in the supplementary material in order to allow replication. In addition, the authors are perhaps too optimistic when stating that “the coincidence between PC1dis short eccentricity and ZB18a astronomical solution indicates that the filtered PC1dis precession signal is a good indicator of precession-related light carbon concentration/CaCO3 dissolution variations” (lines 281-283). The fact that the filtered PC1dis eccentricity signal is similar to the eccentricity solution in ZB18 does not necessarily mean that the precession signal also has to match. In fact, the amplitude of precession cycles does not fit that of eccentricity cycles. In order to reinforce their interpretation, the authors should try to correlate their precession cycles with those from other records. Although there are no precession solutions for the studied time interval (lines 279-280), some studies carried out in partly coeval successions have identified the record of early Eocene precession cycles (e.g., Westerhold et al., 2007, 2017). My impression is that the filtered HIRM-CFB precession signal is probably not reliable, as it displays only five precession cycles in the PETM (Fig. 8), which are too few for the estimated 170-200 ky duration of this event (the 9.5 precession cycles obtained in the filtered PC1dis signal seem to be more reasonable). Consequently, the discussion about the environmental significance of the differences between the filtered PC1dis and HIRM-CFB precession signals seems to be too speculative (lines 285-293). Taking into account that the filtered HIRM-CFB eccentricity signal also departs from the filtered PC1dis and ZB18 eccentricity signals, my impression is that the HIRM-CFB record is not suitable for filtering. This would mean that the discussion about the filtered HIRM-CFB eccentricity signal is also speculative (lines 298-314).
(6) In this work, the authors seem to misunderstand the relationship between eccentricity cycles and seasonal contrast. More specifically, they suggest that eccentricity maxima produce enhanced seasonal contrast (lines 314-315 and 326-327). In reality, seasonal contrast is determined by precession cycles, not by eccentricity cycles. Precessional variations in insolation determine the temperature contrast between summer and winter, along with the consequent annual distribution of precipitation, storminess, organic productivity, etc. In the northern hemisphere, precessional seasonality is minimized (mild summers and winters) when boreal summers occur at aphelion and winters at perihelion (i.e., high precession index), but seasonality increases (warmer summers and cooler winters) when summers occur at perihelion and winters at aphelion (i.e., low precession index). Periodic variations in the eccentricity of the Earth’s orbit modulate the amplitude of precession-driven seasonality. Thus, at eccentricity maxima both maximized and minimized seasonality occur during one single precession cycle. Conversely, during eccentricity minima seasonality remains similar (i.e., intermediate) regardless of the precession index. This should be taken into account in the discussion in lines 315-337. In this regard, it is very unlikely that “eccentricity minima periods … with relatively stable seasonal contrast … produced wetter conditions … which may have enhanced fluvial haematite transport to Contessa” (lines 318-321). Fluvial sediment input increases with seasonality, reaching maximum values under dry subhumid precipitation regimes with three to five wet months per year (Cecil and Dulong, 2003). These conditions generally occur at eccentricity maxima and low precession index. Similarly, rather than the minimum eccentricity configurations suggested in lines 329-333, “amplified seasonal precipitation and intermittent extreme precipitation events” are more likely during high seasonality conditions developed at maximum eccentricity and low precession index.

OTHER ISSUES
There are too many acronyms in the manuscript, making it difficult to read.
Both haematite (text) and hematite (Fig. 5) are used. Please homogenize.
How stratigraphic thickness (Fig. S1) was transformed into age/time (e.g., Fig. 2) should be explained (age model).
Line 61: “short-lived (~200 kyr) carbon cycle perturbations”. Maybe <200 kyr is more appropriate, as most events were significantly shorter than 200 ky and even the PETM was also probably shorter (170-200 kyr).
Lines 73-79: the wet-wetter and dry-drier evolutions may be too simplistic. Hydroclimates changed throughout some hyperthermal events.
Lines 138-139: Most of the other marl levels do seem to coincide with CIEs. In this regard, why was the J event (Fig. S1) not displayed in the other figures? Would it not fit the model and coincide with the long eccentricity maximum at ca. 53.2 Ma in Fig. S2?
Lines 149: The X drop at 300ºC does not occur in EETZ and ETM2, and is rather subtle in pre-ETM2, meaning that it is clearly visible in only 50% of the cases. Furthermore, the Curie temperature of some iron sulphides (e.g., greigite) is also approximately 300ºC. The potential occurrence (or absence) of sulphides should be discussed.
Lines 151-152: If only two out of five cases show the drop in X at 615-630ºC, why is the interpretation extrapolated to “almost ALL Contessa Road samples”?
Lines 186: Fig. 5b, and not 6b.
Lines 210-215: Unclear line of reasoning, please elaborate on this.
Line 220: “Despite the terrigenous origin” (singular).
Line 240-241: All marl layers coincide with positive PC2all positive peaks, not only the so-called “dissolution horizons” (see also comment on lines 138-139).
Line 263: “deduced from” instead of “indicated”.
Lines 288-293: Unclear line of reasoning. Even if this discussion were pertinent (see general comment 5), increased light C and haematite concentrations could also result from increased fresh water (i.e., fluvial) supplies, which would suggest that terrigenous dilution was the main controlling mechanism for the compositional variations observed throughout the succession, rather than variations in carbonate deposition/dissolution (see general comment 3).
Lines 343-345: Unclear, please rephrase.
Line 367: Fig. 9, rather than 8.
Line 378: The 27-kyr recovery of the PETM seems to be subjective, as peak hyperthermal conditions may have been reached significantly earlier according to Fig. 9a.
Lines 403 and 407: Remove “depth” and “depths”, respectively.
Line 416. Use “They” instead of “Piedrahita13”.
Line 495: “Thin”, rather than “thick”?
Line 677: “heating and cooling” … “red and blue”.
Suppl. lines 13-15: Visually it seems that Sr maxima occur at hyperthermals.
Suppl. Lines 55-56: Goethite is a high coercivity mineral. Does this sentence refer to haematite content?
Suppl. line 58: EDXS show elemental occurrences/abundances, but not mineralogy. It cannot be concluded that “clay minerals are compositionally similar across all intervals”.
Suppl. line 69: This section is highly speculative and does not reach any conclusion. Superfluous?
Suppl. lines 80-81: Productivity can increase without higher terrigenous input (e.g., upwelling).
Fig. S4: What do low coercitivy components represent and why are magnetite and maghemite not distinguished? Why is goethite not represented in EELMZ? Mean coercitivity values and dispersion could be included.

Kodama, 2012. Paleomagnetism of Sedimentary Rocks: Process and Interpretation, 157 pp. Wiley-Blackwell, Oxford.
Westerhold et al., 2007. Paleoceanography 22, PA220.
Westerhold et al., 2017. Clim. Past 13, 1129-1152.
reviewer_comments.reviewer_2:
This paper is a high-resolution study of the Palaeocene-Eocene interval in the important and well-studied Contessa Road section in Gubbio, Italy. Although extensive palaeomagnetic, biostratigraphic and isotopic work has been done on this succession, this study uses an environmental magnetic and geochemical approach which allows the authors to infer terrestrial rather than palaeoceanographic conditions. It thus complements a number of papers from around the Tethyan margin examining the terrestrial response to the PETM (e.g. Bolle et al., Schmitz et al., 2003; Schmitz et al., 2007; Dallanave et al., 2012). Few of these studies extend beyond the PETM to a detailed consideration of other Eocene carbon cycle perturbation events, and this is an important contribution of this paper.

The main findings of this paper are as follows:
A. There was a long-term aridification of the western Tethys over 58-52 Ma
B. This was punctuated by carbon cycle perturbations which produced even drier conditions
C. Recovery from these perturbations to pre-event hydroclimate conditions consistently took 23-27 kyr, regardless of the size of the perturbation

These arguments are underpinned by an interpretation of the magnetic mineral content of the sediments as follows:
1. The magnetic fraction is primarily composed of maghemite and pigmentary hematite, both of which are primarily detrital
2. Absolute concentration of both high and low-coercivity components with respect to overall non-carbonate content shows a long-term decrease, but hematite:maghemite ratio shows a long-term increase
3. Hematite:maghemite ratio also increases during some of the hyperthermals and short carbon-cycle perturbations
4. Reduced overall magnetic fraction and increased hematite proportion is inferred to indicate aridity

My main comments are some questions about points 1 and 4, some consideration of the interpretation of principal components, and an assessment of the findings on the basis of interpretations 1-4.
Following this I have appended line-by-line comments.

1. The magnetic fraction is primarily composed of maghemite and pigmentary hematite, both of which are primarily detrital
This is argued on the basis of Figure 3, which shows temperature-dependence of magnetic susceptibility and 3-component thermal demagnetisation diagrams for selected samples. It is argued that “almost all” Contessa Road samples show evidence of maghemite as a fall in MS around 300C (maghemite converting to hematite) and/or a fall in MS around 625C (maghemite Curie temperature). On the basis of the six samples shown, I can see these features in only three (PETM initial phase, PETM recovery phase, and EELMZ, which is subsequently discussed only in the supplementary information). Meanwhile, it is mentioned that two of the samples (PETM recovery and Pre-ETM 2) show evidence for magnetite, which I agree with. I would also interpret EETZ, ETM2 and EELMZ as potentially indicating magnetite. It may be that all or almost all of the samples not shown here contain the two features associated with maghemite – if this is the basis for the statement, it should be explicitly stated and perhaps quantified (what percentage of the samples show these features).

The 3-component thermal demagnetisation is said to show a pigmentary hematite signature (gradual demagnetisation to 675C), with the exception of the EELMZ. I found this convincing. It seems to me there is also some evidence of magnetite in PETM recovery and EETZ.

I note that previous publications on the same outcrop, as well as on other outcrops of broadly the same formation, have also inferred a mixture of hematite, magnetite and maghemite. However, much more weight has previously been given to the contribution of both biogenic and detrital magnetite in lower parts of this succession (Abrejevitch et al., 2015; Coccioni et al., 2019), both of which are largely dismissed here. A previous study of this succession inferred that the hematite is primarily early post-depositional and authigenic, a possibility which is not discussed here (Abrejevitch et al., 2015). The maghemite could also be pre- or post-depositional oxidation of either detrital or biogenic magnetite, which is again not considered here.

Overall, I think that given the importance of the detrital origin and mineralogy of the magnetic fraction to the argument in later parts of the paper, more could be done here to discuss possible other interpretations of the magnetic results and explain why they are not preferred. The supplementary material makes reference to IRM unmixing curves. It is interesting that these curves show fewer components than similar analyses for older parts of the Contessa Road section (Abrejevitch et al., 2015; Coccioni et al., 2019). These data could potentially help to test the argument that the soft component is primarily detrital rather than biogenic.

2. Absolute concentration of both high and low-coercivity components with respect to overall non-carbonate content shows a long-term decrease, but hematite:maghemite ratio shows a long-term increase
This seems convincingly demonstrated by Figure 5.

3. Hematite:maghemite ratio also increases during some of the hyperthermals and short carbon-cycle perturbations
Again, this is convincingly demonstrated by Figure 5 and Figure 9, although there are other short-lived increases of similar magnitude which do not coincide with carbon-cycle perturbations.

4. Reduced overall magnetic fraction and increased hematite proportion is inferred to indicate aridity
The argument made here is that aridity in the source area led to reduced ferrihydrite formation, thus reducing the possibility of subsequent formation of maghemite and then hematite. However, the aridity promoted the formation of hematite from any ferrihydrite or maghemite that was formed, thus producing a situation where both magnetic components were reduced in absolute terms but the ratio of hematite to maghemite increased. This makes a number of assumptions: 1. that the magnetic signal is controlled almost entirely by input of detrital maghemite and hematite. 2. That the detrital maghemite comes almost entirely from ferrihydrite oxidation rather than oxidation of detrital or pedogenic magnetite. 3. That the signal is a proxy for source area soil conditions. 1 and 2 are discussed above. The third assumption leaves out the possibility of post-depositional reductive dissolution in the sediments, which would similarly both reduce the overall magnetic content and increase the hematite/maghemite ratio, due to the lower stability of maghemite in these conditions. A variation on this (with the dissolution occurring prior to deposition) is proposed by Abrejevitch et al. (2015) for a similar (though more extreme) set of magnetic features in the Gubbio section below the K-Pg boundary. The hypothesis of source area aridity is plausible, but as with the identification of the minerals, I think it is important to discuss other possibilities and explain why this one is preferred.

Interpretation of Principal Components
Several parts of the argument are based on the interpretation of principal components. PC1(dis) is interpreted as primarily representing carbonate dissolution. I see no issue with this, and this interpretation is backed up by previous studies of this section (e.g. Galeotti et al., 2010). PC1(all) is also interpreted as representing carbonate dissolution. This is more interesting, as the magnetic concentration parameters relative to detrital input are all positively loaded on this PC, suggesting that during periods of reduced net carbonate sedimentation, either detrital sediments became more magnetic (perhaps due to increased ferrihydrite -> maghemite -> hematite and/or increased production of pedogenic magnetite) or there was an alternate process which increased the magnetic mineral fraction relative to the detrital fraction as a whole. This is similar to the pattern seen in Coccioni et al (2019), which they interpreted as increased biogenic magnetite production by magnetotactic bacteria due to high nutrient levels. Given the importance of Bcr and S-ratio to the later arguments about aridity, it would be interesting to see a PCA(all) that also included these parameters.

The interpretation of PC2(all) is interesting. In L242-245 it is argued that the fact that CFB magnetic mineral parameters and Ca both show negative loadings on this PC indicates that there was also significant terrigenous input during times of reduced carbonate dissolution. However, the elements identified as proxies for terrigenous input are positively loaded on this PC, i.e. anticorrelated to the magnetic parameters and Ca, so the interpretation of this as representing increased terrigenous input seems unsupported. What this seems to me to indicate is that the underlying process was something that resulted in reduced terrigenous/increased carbonate input but simultaneously in magnetic enhancement of the non-carbonate fraction. I note that the loadings of the magnetic parameters on this PC are quite low, and the discussion does not return to PC2(all) again, so perhaps a detailed consideration is not so important. However, I do think the current interpretation should be revised.

The most important PC interpretation from the point of view of the main arguments of the paper is PC1(arid), which represents the anticorrelation between overall magnetic concentration (including absolute carbonate-free concentrations of all coercivity components) and proportion of the magnetic fraction represented by harder minerals (implicitly hematite). This is the basis of the argument discussed above in point 4, and so I will not discuss it further here.

Returning to the findings:
A. Long-term aridification of the western Tethys over 58-52 Ma
If the identification of the magnetic minerals as detrital hematite and maghemite and the interpretation of PC1(arid) as a source area soil aridity signal are both accepted, this is a well-supported finding.

B. Punctuation by carbon cycle perturbations which produced even drier conditions
Based on Figure 9, I can see the argument for increased aridity during the first part of the PETM and the first part of ETM2. L1 and L2 are also convincing. H2 and I1 look pretty marginal, I2 I don’t see at all, and ETM3 seems to be less arid by comparison with the immediately preceding period. F and the final phase of the PETM both seem to have increased humidity. Overall, this is a pretty complicated picture.

C. Recovery from these perturbations to pre-event hydroclimate conditions over 23-27 kyr
This argument is based on three hyperthermals: the PETM, ETM2 and ETM3. Here I think there needs to be a discussion of how the peak of the event is identified and how you identified the point at which conditions returned to pre-event baselines (or indeed, how you quantified pre-event baselines). As it is, the “peak” of the PETM has similar values of PC1(arid) to a prior peak a few tens of thousands of years earlier, and the “recovery to pre-event conditions” is actually a change to conditions significantly more humid than those immediately before the PETM. The peak of ETM2 is clearer, but again, the “recovery” is set at significantly lower aridity that the values immediately before the event. The most arid conditions for ETM3 occur before the onset of the event as indicated by the shaded bar, and the “recovery” is truncated by the intervention of the EELMZ. Given this, I think it is quite speculative to argue that there is a relatively constant time interval over which hyperthermals return to “normal” conditions. If there was a clearer discussion of how these points were identified, it is possible that this problem could be resolved, although I would also emphasise in the text that there are only three data points to go on.

reviewer_comments.reviewer_3:
The study by Piedrahita presented several interesting records of western Tethyan hydroclimate during the early Eocene. Those records are at orbital time scale resolution and contain highly valuable information of sensitivity of western Tethyan hydroclimate to carbon cycle perturbations. Given my expertise, my review only focuses on the staging of this study and discussions of climatic implications of these records.

1. I found the staging of this manuscript a bit problematic. The wet-gets-wetter and dry-gets-dryer paradigm describes the hydroclimate response dominated by tropospheric moistening without changing circulation in response to CO2 increase (Held and Soden, 2006, J. Clim.), which leads to additional moisture being carried away from regions of divergence towards regions of convergence. However, the subtropical drying inferred from this paradigm, which is used to stage this study, only applies to the OCEAN! On land, P>=E in general, which implies either balanced (no net runoff) or slightly converging moisture flux (with net runoff). As a result, increasing tropospheric humidity can only increase or maintain P-E on land (Seager and Vecchi, 2010, PNAS; Byrne and O’Gormon, 2015, J. Clim.). Moreover, key components of subtropical terrestrial hydrological cycle such as monsoons (characterized by summer precip) and Mediterranean climate (characterized by winter precip) are controlled by regional circulation patterns that are departures from the zonal mean Hadley circulation. Tropospheric humidification can lead to enhanced monsoon rainfall even without any change or weakened monsoon circulation (Endo and Kitoh, 2014, GRL). In the Mediterranean region, drying over the land is explained by enhanced mass divergence due to strengthened high pressure system in the nearby region (Seager et al., 2014, J. Clim.). Finally, there is an inherent time scale difference between project future change in hydroclimate and the reconstructed early Eocene hydroclimate change presented here. The former does not involve slow feedback in the climate system such as vegetation and ice sheet (does not apply to this study), which are important for the latter (e.g., Lunt et al., 2010 Nat. Geo., Feng et al., 2022; Nat. Comm.). To me, the introduction and discussion could be revised to more accurately reflect knowledge on terrestrial and particularly Mediterranean hydroclimate as well as a long-term climate change perspective that deep time paleoclimate records can bring.

2. The clarity of the discussion on “Orbitally forced LPEE hydroclimate variability in the western Tethys” could be improved. For example, “short eccentricity maxima” can be more explicitly written as northern hemisphere summer perihelion during the short eccentricity cycle. It is useful to be explicit given that eccentricity by itself does not affect insolation. Also, the linkage between changing seasonal cycle and the mean hydroclimate state was never explained. Kutzbath et al, 2020 (PNAS) might be a good starting point to explain how the seasonal changes in insolation driven by precession cycle can result in mean state changes of precipitation and P-E. They showed a linkage through shifting winter storm track.

Comment 2: Why all magnetic minerals are interpreted to be detrital and why some (e.g., magnetite)
are not (partly) biogenic or authigenic should also be more clearly explained. In addition, pigmentary
haematite in red bed sequences is usually secondary and probably formed in the order of 105-106 years

We have added a section “Origin of Contessa Road magnetic minerals” to address this. Initially, we
discuss the hypothesis of Channell et al. (1982), who suggested that haematite formed at the expense
of goethite during oxic periods. In contrast, periods with reducing settings would have inhibited
maghemite and haematite formation. These variations are not compatible with the LPEE Contessa
Road magnetic mineral record. Furthermore, we now indicate that sedimentary and fossil evidence
reveal reduced organic inputs to the post K/Pg Contessa Road record (Coccioni et al., 2019), and
insignificant reductive diagenesis via organic matter degradation and microbial oxidant consumption
(e.g., Roberts, 2015). Lack of reductive diagenesis also contrasts with the hypothesis of Abrajevitch et
al. (2015), who interpreted that oxic diagenesis following a period of reducing conditions generated
haematite at the expense of detrital Fe oxyhydroxides. This assumption also implies continental Fe
oxyhydroxide transformation (Jiang et al., 2022). Combined evidence indicates that the western Tethys
had dry hydroclimates, which is compatible with haematite rather than goethite formation. Hence, we
suggest that most haematite and maghemite is detrital. Following the reviewer’s suggestion, we also
discuss the possibility of haematite formation via post-depositional alteration of Fe-rich minerals
(Kodama, 2012). We now clarify that this mechanism is not compatible with compositional
enrichments of haematite and lowered magnetic mineral concentrations at Contessa Road. This
supports our interpretation of the detrital origin of haematite (lines 230-288).
Scaglia Rossa carbonates is restricted to central ridges in FORC diagrams and IRM unmixing
components with ~20-50 mT coercivities. These features can also be related to detrital maghemite/
magnetite. Furthermore, conclusive evidence for biogenic magnetite occurrences at Contessa Road

Comment 6: In this work, the authors seem to misunderstand the relationship between eccentricity
cycles and seasonal contrast. More specifically, they suggest that eccentricity maxima produce
enhanced seasonal contrast (lines 314-315 and 326-327). In reality, seasonal contrast is determined by
precession cycles, not by eccentricity cycles. Precessional variations in insolation determine the
temperature contrast between summer and winter, along with the consequent annual distribution of
precipitation, storminess, organic productivity, etc. In the northern hemisphere, precessional
seasonality is minimized (mild summers and winters) when boreal summers occur at aphelion and
winters at perihelion (i.e., high precession index), but seasonality increases (warmer summers and
cooler winters) when summers occur at perihelion and winters at aphelion (i.e., low precession index).
Periodic variations in the eccentricity of the Earth’s orbit modulate the amplitude of precession-driven
seasonality. Thus, at eccentricity maxima both maximized and minimized seasonality occur during
one single precession cycle. Conversely, during eccentricity minima seasonality remains similar (i.e.,
intermediate) regardless of the precession index. This should be taken into account in the discussion
in lines 315-337. In this regard, it is very unlikely that “eccentricity minima periods … with relatively
stable seasonal contrast … produced wetter conditions … which may have enhanced fluvial haematite
transport to Contessa” (lines 318-321). Fluvial sediment input increases with seasonality, reaching
maximum values under dry subhumid precipitation regimes with three to five wet months per year
(Cecil and Dulong, 2003). These conditions generally occur at eccentricity maxima and low precession
index. Similarly, rather than the minimum eccentricity configurations suggested in lines 329-333,
“amplified seasonal precipitation and intermittent extreme precipitation events” are more likely during
high seasonality conditions developed at maximum eccentricity and low precession index.

expression, which enhanced seasonal contrast. We suggest that these conditions, and short-lived
carbon cycle perturbations, intensified the hydrological cycle and produced orbitally paced dry
conditions in short eccentricity timescales (lines 330-432).

Reviewer 1 Comment 2
The reviewer comments that with respect to the magnetic minerals, there are some major questions
outstanding:
1. Could the haematite and maghemite be authigenic?
2. Could the haematite be late diagenetic?
3. Could the magnetite be biogenic?

1. Could the haematite and maghemite be authigenic?
Previous models for the alternation between red (haematite-rich) and white (haematite-poor)
lithologies at this site have argued for an authigenic origin for the haematite, as follows: model 1
(Channel et al., 1982) suggests that intervals with reducing conditions did not produce haematite
while those with oxic conditions did; model 2 (Abrajevitch et al., 2015) suggests haematite was
formed in intervals that were subject to reducing conditions followed by oxic conditions. The authors
argue that neither of these models can be applied to the late Palaeocene-early Eocene interval due to
the lack of any evidence for reducing conditions in either the white or the red units (no iron sulphides,
no evidence for major organic carbon input). Furthermore, the white lithology contains maghemite but
not haematite, which differs from the magnetic assemblage present in white lithologies underpinning
model 2, and is incompatible with reducing conditions.
I am convinced by this argument with respect to the white lithology. Given that in order to form
pigmentary haematite in subaqueous sediments, there must be dissolved iron in the pore waters, and
that this iron is usually argued to proceed from dissolution deeper in the sediment due to reducing
conditions, this would also seem to support the authors’ argument that the pigmentary haematite in
the overlying intervals is not authigenic. I note that one of the arguments in favour of an authigenic
origin for the pigmentary haematite in Channel et al. (1982) is that colours sometimes change within
bedding units – I wonder if this occurs in the interval studied here? If not, this could be noted for
further support.

2. Could the haematite be late diagenetic?
Reviewer 1 notes that pigmentary haematite is considered to usually form 105-106 years after
deposition. The authors argue that this cannot be the case here because the proportion of haematite
increases as the overall magnetic content decreases, which seems reasonable. This argument could be
strengthened by including references to other marine intervals where detrital pigmentary haematite
has been inferred.

3. Could the magnetite be biogenic?
The authors have done significant work to address the possibility of biogenic magnetite in the section.
This is a very difficult question to solve without a positive TEM ID; however, the IRM unmixing work is
a good approach and indicates that the main low-coercivity signal is likely to be detrital. Another way
to support this might be to consider what effect the biogenic magnetite might have on the story if it is
present. For example, subtracting the proportions of the low-coercivity signal that could potentially be
biogenic magnetite in each interval and seeing if it makes a major difference to the overall patterns.
Just eyeballing it it looks like any potential biogenic contribution is higher in the later periods, so
would be more likely to strengthen the observed trend of reduced low coercivity/increased high
coercivity rather than weaken it.

Overall, with the respect to Reviewer 1 Comment 2, I think the authors have done the important work
of clarifying their reasoning so that the reader can judge for themselves. While they could potentially
add one or two more lines of evidence, I do not think this is indispensable and leave it up to the editor
to decide.

Reviewer 1 questions the connections drawn between the precession and eccentricity signals in PC1dis
and HIRM-CFB and seasonality, noting that in the Northern Hemisphere, maximum precession =
minimum seasonality and minimum precession = maximum seasonality. Eccentricity modulates this,
with maximum eccentricity producing both maximum and minimum seasonalities in a given precession
cycle, while minimum eccentricity produces little contrast in seasonality across a given precession
cycle. Reviewer 1 further notes that seasonal precipitation, extreme precipitation events and fluvial
input increase with increased seasonality.
The discussion in lines 370-385 of the revised MS is consistent with this, with maximum precession
argued to represent times of greater aridity/higher HIRM-CFB, and vice versa. However, the discussion
in lines 388-402 as well as the response to the reviewer do not seem to have taken the reviewer’s
concerns into account. Maximum eccentricity is still identified as producing maximum seasonal
contrast in lines 394-395, although the reviewer’s point was that maximum eccentricity modulates
precession such that both maximum seasonal contrast and minimum seasonal contrast occur (in the
Northern Hemisphere, at minimum and maximum precession, respectively). Thus, given that most of
the LPEEs last for several precession cycles, they cannot be said to be simply times of maximum
seasonal contrast.
The authors also argue in lines 396-397 that maximum seasonal contrast at eccentricity maxima
produces dry conditions/reduced seasonal precipitation, although they have argued the opposite in
lines 370-385 (maximum seasonal contrast = wetter conditions/increased seasonal precipitation,
consistent with Reviewer 1 and, e.g., Bosmans et al., 2015). This identification of eccentricity maxima
with enhanced seasonal contrast is repeated in lines 410-411. If high seasonal contrast is considered
to produce overall wetter conditions due to enhanced seasonal and monsoonal precipitation and
increased extreme precipitation events, as argued in lines 370-385, then periods of maximum
eccentricity should be characterised by both enhanced dry (maximum precession/minimum seasonal
contrast/minimum seasonal precipitation) and enhanced wet (minimum precipitation/maximum seasonal
contrast/maximum seasonal precipitation) conditions. I could see an argument where the
haematite precursors are produced during the wet periods and then the haematite itself is produced
and transported during the dry periods, and thus the enhancement of both types of climate during
eccentricity maxima and LPEEs results in overall increased average haematite in the sediments. I
could also see an argument where the increased temperatures during LPEEs enhance the increase in
haematite formation and transport at times of minimum seasonal contrast (and therefore minimum
seasonal precipitation), which would also occur at times of maximum eccentricity. However, at
present, the argument about how eccentricity modulation of precession produces the observed
haematite variations is not clear to me.

### Reviewer 1

This study analyses the concentrations and properties of magnetic minerals from the lower Eocene Contessa road section (Italy) in order to deduce the paleoenvironmental and paleoclimatic evolution of the western Mediterranean area. The manuscript confirms the results from previous studies carried out in this section and elsewhere, which showed that pelagic sedimentation in the area was astronomically forced and several short-lived (<200 ky-long) carbon-cycle perturbations occurred when long and short eccentricity maxima overlapped. Additionally, the authors found that western Mediterranean conditions became generally drier as the early Eocene climate became progressively warmer (eventually leading to the early Eocene climatic optimum), although this trend was interrupted during a ~500 ky-long wetter interval at approximately 55 Ma. They also deduce that extremely dry conditions occurred during the short-lived carbon cycle perturbations and that the recovery to pre-event conditions was fast (23-27 ky). They suggest that these results may be relevant to our understanding of the evolution and impact of anthropogenic global warming.

The manuscript is a potentially good fit for the journal and its readers. The authors have gone to great lengths with their research and show a sound understanding of the subject. However, there are some loose ends and there is room for improvement in terms of methodology and how the results are interpreted and presented.

MAJOR ISSUES
(1) It is not clear how CFB parameters were obtained. For example, was the carbonate content of each sample separated using physicochemical treatments in the laboratory (i.e., were samples decarbonated) and were the mineralogical properties of the residue subsequently analysed? Alternatively, was the carbonate content subtracted by theoretical calculations? The method used should be more clearly explained. The former method would probably also allow for the identification of clay and magnetic mineral phases by X ray diffraction, which would help to support (or refute) some of the authors’ interpretations.
(2) Why all magnetic minerals are interpreted to be detrital and why some (e.g., magnetite) are not (partly) biogenic or authigenic should also be more clearly explained. In addition, pigmentary haematite in red bed sequences is usually secondary and probably formed in the order of 105-106 years after deposition (Kodama, 2012). Could this affect the interpretation of shorter hydroclimate variations?
(3) From the very beginning (line 108) the authors state that the variations in the carbonate/clay ratio throughout the succession record variations in the rate of carbonate deposition or dissolution, later favouring dissolution as the main controlling factor (line 227). The line of reasoning should be more clearly explained. Initially, they ignore that clay (and magnetic mineral) content could also vary as a consequence of changes in the rate of terrigenous sediment input over time (i.e., terrigenous dilution). This possibility is only considered later in the manuscript, and restricted to the interpretation of the EETZ (lines 241-248). In order to address these issues further, the authors could obtain some terrigenous input proxies (e.g., Ti/Al and Zr/Al ratios) throughout the succession.
(4) PCA2all scores are used as a proxy of variations in the rates of detrital input and CaCO3 dissolution over time. However, each of the factors identified by the PCA analysis should represent only one controlling mechanism, not two (i.e., PCA2all should represent variations in either detrital input or CaCO3 dissolution, but not in both). Furthermore, both Ca (i.e., carbonates) and magnetic parameters show negative loadings in PCA2all, suggesting that they are related. Consequently, why do the authors relate negative PCA2all values only with detrital supplies in Fig. 6e? Why does Ca increase in EETZ? In addition, matrices of all PCA analyses (tables with loadings between variables and principal components) should also be provided in the supplementary material in order to know which variables are relevant to each component and their statistical significance.
(5) Regarding spectral analysis and orbital forcing, it should be emphasized that the power spectra are rather noisy and spiky (Fig. 7), meaning that there are significant periodicities that the authors seem to ignore. The original data used for the spectral analysis should be provided in the supplementary material in order to allow replication. In addition, the authors are perhaps too optimistic when stating that “the coincidence between PC1dis short eccentricity and ZB18a astronomical solution indicates that the filtered PC1dis precession signal is a good indicator of precession-related light carbon concentration/CaCO3 dissolution variations” (lines 281-283). The fact that the filtered PC1dis eccentricity signal is similar to the eccentricity solution in ZB18 does not necessarily mean that the precession signal also has to match. In fact, the amplitude of precession cycles does not fit that of eccentricity cycles. In order to reinforce their interpretation, the authors should try to correlate their precession cycles with those from other records. Although there are no precession solutions for the studied time interval (lines 279-280), some studies carried out in partly coeval successions have identified the record of early Eocene precession cycles (e.g., Westerhold et al., 2007, 2017). My impression is that the filtered HIRM-CFB precession signal is probably not reliable, as it displays only five precession cycles in the PETM (Fig. 8), which are too few for the estimated 170-200 ky duration of this event (the 9.5 precession cycles obtained in the filtered PC1dis signal seem to be more reasonable). Consequently, the discussion about the environmental significance of the differences between the filtered PC1dis and HIRM-CFB precession signals seems to be too speculative (lines 285-293). Taking into account that the filtered HIRM-CFB eccentricity signal also departs from the filtered PC1dis and ZB18 eccentricity signals, my impression is that the HIRM-CFB record is not suitable for filtering. This would mean that the discussion about the filtered HIRM-CFB eccentricity signal is also speculative (lines 298-314).
(6) In this work, the authors seem to misunderstand the relationship between eccentricity cycles and seasonal contrast. More specifically, they suggest that eccentricity maxima produce enhanced seasonal contrast (lines 314-315 and 326-327). In reality, seasonal contrast is determined by precession cycles, not by eccentricity cycles. Precessional variations in insolation determine the temperature contrast between summer and winter, along with the consequent annual distribution of precipitation, storminess, organic productivity, etc. In the northern hemisphere, precessional seasonality is minimized (mild summers and winters) when boreal summers occur at aphelion and winters at perihelion (i.e., high precession index), but seasonality increases (warmer summers and cooler winters) when summers occur at perihelion and winters at aphelion (i.e., low precession index). Periodic variations in the eccentricity of the Earth’s orbit modulate the amplitude of precession-driven seasonality. Thus, at eccentricity maxima both maximized and minimized seasonality occur during one single precession cycle. Conversely, during eccentricity minima seasonality remains similar (i.e., intermediate) regardless of the precession index. This should be taken into account in the discussion in lines 315-337. In this regard, it is very unlikely that “eccentricity minima periods … with relatively stable seasonal contrast … produced wetter conditions … which may have enhanced fluvial haematite transport to Contessa” (lines 318-321). Fluvial sediment input increases with seasonality, reaching maximum values under dry subhumid precipitation regimes with three to five wet months per year (Cecil and Dulong, 2003). These conditions generally occur at eccentricity maxima and low precession index. Similarly, rather than the minimum eccentricity configurations suggested in lines 329-333, “amplified seasonal precipitation and intermittent extreme precipitation events” are more likely during high seasonality conditions developed at maximum eccentricity and low precession index.

### Reviewer 2

This paper is a high-resolution study of the Palaeocene-Eocene interval in the important and well-studied Contessa Road section in Gubbio, Italy. Although extensive palaeomagnetic, biostratigraphic and isotopic work has been done on this succession, this study uses an environmental magnetic and geochemical approach which allows the authors to infer terrestrial rather than palaeoceanographic conditions. It thus complements a number of papers from around the Tethyan margin examining the terrestrial response to the PETM (e.g. Bolle et al., Schmitz et al., 2003; Schmitz et al., 2007; Dallanave et al., 2012). Few of these studies extend beyond the PETM to a detailed consideration of other Eocene carbon cycle perturbation events, and this is an important contribution of this paper.

The main findings of this paper are as follows:
A. There was a long-term aridification of the western Tethys over 58-52 Ma
B. This was punctuated by carbon cycle perturbations which produced even drier conditions
C. Recovery from these perturbations to pre-event hydroclimate conditions consistently took 23-27 kyr, regardless of the size of the perturbation

These arguments are underpinned by an interpretation of the magnetic mineral content of the sediments as follows:
1. The magnetic fraction is primarily composed of maghemite and pigmentary hematite, both of which are primarily detrital
2. Absolute concentration of both high and low-coercivity components with respect to overall non-carbonate content shows a long-term decrease, but hematite:maghemite ratio shows a long-term increase
3. Hematite:maghemite ratio also increases during some of the hyperthermals and short carbon-cycle perturbations
4. Reduced overall magnetic fraction and increased hematite proportion is inferred to indicate aridity

My main comments are some questions about points 1 and 4, some consideration of the interpretation of principal components, and an assessment of the findings on the basis of interpretations 1-4.
Following this I have appended line-by-line comments.

1. The magnetic fraction is primarily composed of maghemite and pigmentary hematite, both of which are primarily detrital
This is argued on the basis of Figure 3, which shows temperature-dependence of magnetic susceptibility and 3-component thermal demagnetisation diagrams for selected samples. It is argued that “almost all” Contessa Road samples show evidence of maghemite as a fall in MS around 300C (maghemite converting to hematite) and/or a fall in MS around 625C (maghemite Curie temperature). On the basis of the six samples shown, I can see these features in only three (PETM initial phase, PETM recovery phase, and EELMZ, which is subsequently discussed only in the supplementary information). Meanwhile, it is mentioned that two of the samples (PETM recovery and Pre-ETM 2) show evidence for magnetite, which I agree with. I would also interpret EETZ, ETM2 and EELMZ as potentially indicating magnetite. It may be that all or almost all of the samples not shown here contain the two features associated with maghemite – if this is the basis for the statement, it should be explicitly stated and perhaps quantified (what percentage of the samples show these features).

The 3-component thermal demagnetisation is said to show a pigmentary hematite signature (gradual demagnetisation to 675C), with the exception of the EELMZ. I found this convincing. It seems to me there is also some evidence of magnetite in PETM recovery and EETZ.

I note that previous publications on the same outcrop, as well as on other outcrops of broadly the same formation, have also inferred a mixture of hematite, magnetite and maghemite. However, much more weight has previously been given to the contribution of both biogenic and detrital magnetite in lower parts of this succession (Abrejevitch et al., 2015; Coccioni et al., 2019), both of which are largely dismissed here. A previous study of this succession inferred that the hematite is primarily early post-depositional and authigenic, a possibility which is not discussed here (Abrejevitch et al., 2015). The maghemite could also be pre- or post-depositional oxidation of either detrital or biogenic magnetite, which is again not considered here.

Overall, I think that given the importance of the detrital origin and mineralogy of the magnetic fraction to the argument in later parts of the paper, more could be done here to discuss possible other interpretations of the magnetic results and explain why they are not preferred. The supplementary material makes reference to IRM unmixing curves. It is interesting that these curves show fewer components than similar analyses for older parts of the Contessa Road section (Abrejevitch et al., 2015; Coccioni et al., 2019). These data could potentially help to test the argument that the soft component is primarily detrital rather than biogenic.

2. Absolute concentration of both high and low-coercivity components with respect to overall non-carbonate content shows a long-term decrease, but hematite:maghemite ratio shows a long-term increase
This seems convincingly demonstrated by Figure 5.

3. Hematite:maghemite ratio also increases during some of the hyperthermals and short carbon-cycle perturbations
Again, this is convincingly demonstrated by Figure 5 and Figure 9, although there are other short-lived increases of similar magnitude which do not coincide with carbon-cycle perturbations.

4. Reduced overall magnetic fraction and increased hematite proportion is inferred to indicate aridity
The argument made here is that aridity in the source area led to reduced ferrihydrite formation, thus reducing the possibility of subsequent formation of maghemite and then hematite. However, the aridity promoted the formation of hematite from any ferrihydrite or maghemite that was formed, thus producing a situation where both magnetic components were reduced in absolute terms but the ratio of hematite to maghemite increased. This makes a number of assumptions: 1. that the magnetic signal is controlled almost entirely by input of detrital maghemite and hematite. 2. That the detrital maghemite comes almost entirely from ferrihydrite oxidation rather than oxidation of detrital or pedogenic magnetite. 3. That the signal is a proxy for source area soil conditions. 1 and 2 are discussed above. The third assumption leaves out the possibility of post-depositional reductive dissolution in the sediments, which would similarly both reduce the overall magnetic content and increase the hematite/maghemite ratio, due to the lower stability of maghemite in these conditions. A variation on this (with the dissolution occurring prior to deposition) is proposed by Abrejevitch et al. (2015) for a similar (though more extreme) set of magnetic features in the Gubbio section below the K-Pg boundary. The hypothesis of source area aridity is plausible, but as with the identification of the minerals, I think it is important to discuss other possibilities and explain why this one is preferred.

Interpretation of Principal Components
Several parts of the argument are based on the interpretation of principal components. PC1(dis) is interpreted as primarily representing carbonate dissolution. I see no issue with this, and this interpretation is backed up by previous studies of this section (e.g. Galeotti et al., 2010). PC1(all) is also interpreted as representing carbonate dissolution. This is more interesting, as the magnetic concentration parameters relative to detrital input are all positively loaded on this PC, suggesting that during periods of reduced net carbonate sedimentation, either detrital sediments became more magnetic (perhaps due to increased ferrihydrite -> maghemite -> hematite and/or increased production of pedogenic magnetite) or there was an alternate process which increased the magnetic mineral fraction relative to the detrital fraction as a whole. This is similar to the pattern seen in Coccioni et al (2019), which they interpreted as increased biogenic magnetite production by magnetotactic bacteria due to high nutrient levels. Given the importance of Bcr and S-ratio to the later arguments about aridity, it would be interesting to see a PCA(all) that also included these parameters.

The interpretation of PC2(all) is interesting. In L242-245 it is argued that the fact that CFB magnetic mineral parameters and Ca both show negative loadings on this PC indicates that there was also significant terrigenous input during times of reduced carbonate dissolution. However, the elements identified as proxies for terrigenous input are positively loaded on this PC, i.e. anticorrelated to the magnetic parameters and Ca, so the interpretation of this as representing increased terrigenous input seems unsupported. What this seems to me to indicate is that the underlying process was something that resulted in reduced terrigenous/increased carbonate input but simultaneously in magnetic enhancement of the non-carbonate fraction. I note that the loadings of the magnetic parameters on this PC are quite low, and the discussion does not return to PC2(all) again, so perhaps a detailed consideration is not so important. However, I do think the current interpretation should be revised.

The most important PC interpretation from the point of view of the main arguments of the paper is PC1(arid), which represents the anticorrelation between overall magnetic concentration (including absolute carbonate-free concentrations of all coercivity components) and proportion of the magnetic fraction represented by harder minerals (implicitly hematite). This is the basis of the argument discussed above in point 4, and so I will not discuss it further here.

Returning to the findings:
A. Long-term aridification of the western Tethys over 58-52 Ma
If the identification of the magnetic minerals as detrital hematite and maghemite and the interpretation of PC1(arid) as a source area soil aridity signal are both accepted, this is a well-supported finding.

B. Punctuation by carbon cycle perturbations which produced even drier conditions
Based on Figure 9, I can see the argument for increased aridity during the first part of the PETM and the first part of ETM2. L1 and L2 are also convincing. H2 and I1 look pretty marginal, I2 I don’t see at all, and ETM3 seems to be less arid by comparison with the immediately preceding period. F and the final phase of the PETM both seem to have increased humidity. Overall, this is a pretty complicated picture.

C. Recovery from these perturbations to pre-event hydroclimate conditions over 23-27 kyr
This argument is based on three hyperthermals: the PETM, ETM2 and ETM3. Here I think there needs to be a discussion of how the peak of the event is identified and how you identified the point at which conditions returned to pre-event baselines (or indeed, how you quantified pre-event baselines). As it is, the “peak” of the PETM has similar values of PC1(arid) to a prior peak a few tens of thousands of years earlier, and the “recovery to pre-event conditions” is actually a change to conditions significantly more humid than those immediately before the PETM. The peak of ETM2 is clearer, but again, the “recovery” is set at significantly lower aridity that the values immediately before the event. The most arid conditions for ETM3 occur before the onset of the event as indicated by the shaded bar, and the “recovery” is truncated by the intervention of the EELMZ. Given this, I think it is quite speculative to argue that there is a relatively constant time interval over which hyperthermals return to “normal” conditions. If there was a clearer discussion of how these points were identified, it is possible that this problem could be resolved, although I would also emphasise in the text that there are only three data points to go on.

### Reviewer 3

The study by Piedrahita presented several interesting records of western Tethyan hydroclimate during the early Eocene. Those records are at orbital time scale resolution and contain highly valuable information of sensitivity of western Tethyan hydroclimate to carbon cycle perturbations. Given my expertise, my review only focuses on the staging of this study and discussions of climatic implications of these records.

1. I found the staging of this manuscript a bit problematic. The wet-gets-wetter and dry-gets-dryer paradigm describes the hydroclimate response dominated by tropospheric moistening without changing circulation in response to CO2 increase (Held and Soden, 2006, J. Clim.), which leads to additional moisture being carried away from regions of divergence towards regions of convergence. However, the subtropical drying inferred from this paradigm, which is used to stage this study, only applies to the OCEAN! On land, P>=E in general, which implies either balanced (no net runoff) or slightly converging moisture flux (with net runoff). As a result, increasing tropospheric humidity can only increase or maintain P-E on land (Seager and Vecchi, 2010, PNAS; Byrne and O’Gormon, 2015, J. Clim.). Moreover, key components of subtropical terrestrial hydrological cycle such as monsoons (characterized by summer precip) and Mediterranean climate (characterized by winter precip) are controlled by regional circulation patterns that are departures from the zonal mean Hadley circulation. Tropospheric humidification can lead to enhanced monsoon rainfall even without any change or weakened monsoon circulation (Endo and Kitoh, 2014, GRL). In the Mediterranean region, drying over the land is explained by enhanced mass divergence due to strengthened high pressure system in the nearby region (Seager et al., 2014, J. Clim.). Finally, there is an inherent time scale difference between project future change in hydroclimate and the reconstructed early Eocene hydroclimate change presented here. The former does not involve slow feedback in the climate system such as vegetation and ice sheet (does not apply to this study), which are important for the latter (e.g., Lunt et al., 2010 Nat. Geo., Feng et al., 2022; Nat. Comm.). To me, the introduction and discussion could be revised to more accurately reflect knowledge on terrestrial and particularly Mediterranean hydroclimate as well as a long-term climate change perspective that deep time paleoclimate records can bring.

2. The clarity of the discussion on “Orbitally forced LPEE hydroclimate variability in the western Tethys” could be improved. For example, “short eccentricity maxima” can be more explicitly written as northern hemisphere summer perihelion during the short eccentricity cycle. It is useful to be explicit given that eccentricity by itself does not affect insolation. Also, the linkage between changing seasonal cycle and the mean hydroclimate state was never explained. Kutzbath et al, 2020 (PNAS) might be a good starting point to explain how the seasonal changes in insolation driven by precession cycle can result in mean state changes of precipitation and P-E. They showed a linkage through shifting winter storm track.

Comment 6: In this work, the authors seem to misunderstand the relationship between eccentricity
cycles and seasonal contrast. More specifically, they suggest that eccentricity maxima produce
enhanced seasonal contrast (lines 314-315 and 326-327). In reality, seasonal contrast is determined by
precession cycles, not by eccentricity cycles. Precessional variations in insolation determine the
temperature contrast between summer and winter, along with the consequent annual distribution of
precipitation, storminess, organic productivity, etc. In the northern hemisphere, precessional
seasonality is minimized (mild summers and winters) when boreal summers occur at aphelion and
winters at perihelion (i.e., high precession index), but seasonality increases (warmer summers and
cooler winters) when summers occur at perihelion and winters at aphelion (i.e., low precession index).
Periodic variations in the eccentricity of the Earth’s orbit modulate the amplitude of precession-driven
seasonality. Thus, at eccentricity maxima both maximized and minimized seasonality occur during
one single precession cycle. Conversely, during eccentricity minima seasonality remains similar (i.e.,
intermediate) regardless of the precession index. This should be taken into account in the discussion
in lines 315-337. In this regard, it is very unlikely that “eccentricity minima periods … with relatively
stable seasonal contrast … produced wetter conditions … which may have enhanced fluvial haematite
transport to Contessa” (lines 318-321). Fluvial sediment input increases with seasonality, reaching
maximum values under dry subhumid precipitation regimes with three to five wet months per year
(Cecil and Dulong, 2003). These conditions generally occur at eccentricity maxima and low precession
index. Similarly, rather than the minimum eccentricity configurations suggested in lines 329-333,
“amplified seasonal precipitation and intermittent extreme precipitation events” are more likely during
high seasonality conditions developed at maximum eccentricity and low precession index.

Reviewer 1 Comment 2
The reviewer comments that with respect to the magnetic minerals, there are some major questions
outstanding:
1. Could the haematite and maghemite be authigenic?
2. Could the haematite be late diagenetic?
3. Could the magnetite be biogenic?

1. Could the haematite and maghemite be authigenic?
Previous models for the alternation between red (haematite-rich) and white (haematite-poor)
lithologies at this site have argued for an authigenic origin for the haematite, as follows: model 1
(Channel et al., 1982) suggests that intervals with reducing conditions did not produce haematite
while those with oxic conditions did; model 2 (Abrajevitch et al., 2015) suggests haematite was
formed in intervals that were subject to reducing conditions followed by oxic conditions. The authors
argue that neither of these models can be applied to the late Palaeocene-early Eocene interval due to
the lack of any evidence for reducing conditions in either the white or the red units (no iron sulphides,
no evidence for major organic carbon input). Furthermore, the white lithology contains maghemite but
not haematite, which differs from the magnetic assemblage present in white lithologies underpinning
model 2, and is incompatible with reducing conditions.
I am convinced by this argument with respect to the white lithology. Given that in order to form
pigmentary haematite in subaqueous sediments, there must be dissolved iron in the pore waters, and
that this iron is usually argued to proceed from dissolution deeper in the sediment due to reducing
conditions, this would also seem to support the authors’ argument that the pigmentary haematite in
the overlying intervals is not authigenic. I note that one of the arguments in favour of an authigenic
origin for the pigmentary haematite in Channel et al. (1982) is that colours sometimes change within
bedding units – I wonder if this occurs in the interval studied here? If not, this could be noted for
further support.

2. Could the haematite be late diagenetic?
Reviewer 1 notes that pigmentary haematite is considered to usually form 105-106 years after
deposition. The authors argue that this cannot be the case here because the proportion of haematite
increases as the overall magnetic content decreases, which seems reasonable. This argument could be
strengthened by including references to other marine intervals where detrital pigmentary haematite
has been inferred.

3. Could the magnetite be biogenic?
The authors have done significant work to address the possibility of biogenic magnetite in the section.
This is a very difficult question to solve without a positive TEM ID; however, the IRM unmixing work is
a good approach and indicates that the main low-coercivity signal is likely to be detrital. Another way
to support this might be to consider what effect the biogenic magnetite might have on the story if it is
present. For example, subtracting the proportions of the low-coercivity signal that could potentially be
biogenic magnetite in each interval and seeing if it makes a major difference to the overall patterns.
Just eyeballing it it looks like any potential biogenic contribution is higher in the later periods, so
would be more likely to strengthen the observed trend of reduced low coercivity/increased high
coercivity rather than weaken it.

Overall, with the respect to Reviewer 1 Comment 2, I think the authors have done the important work
of clarifying their reasoning so that the reader can judge for themselves. While they could potentially
add one or two more lines of evidence, I do not think this is indispensable and leave it up to the editor
to decide.

1. Processes for the two PCs are independent
2. Only one process is invoked for each PC

Reviewer 1 comment 6: Climatic interpretation of spectral analysis.
Reviewer 1 questions the connections drawn between the precession and eccentricity signals in PC1dis
and HIRM-CFB and seasonality, noting that in the Northern Hemisphere, maximum precession =
minimum seasonality and minimum precession = maximum seasonality. Eccentricity modulates this,
with maximum eccentricity producing both maximum and minimum seasonalities in a given precession
cycle, while minimum eccentricity produces little contrast in seasonality across a given precession
cycle. Reviewer 1 further notes that seasonal precipitation, extreme precipitation events and fluvial
input increase with increased seasonality.
The discussion in lines 370-385 of the revised MS is consistent with this, with maximum precession
argued to represent times of greater aridity/higher HIRM-CFB, and vice versa. However, the discussion
in lines 388-402 as well as the response to the reviewer do not seem to have taken the reviewer’s
concerns into account. Maximum eccentricity is still identified as producing maximum seasonal
contrast in lines 394-395, although the reviewer’s point was that maximum eccentricity modulates
precession such that both maximum seasonal contrast and minimum seasonal contrast occur (in the
Northern Hemisphere, at minimum and maximum precession, respectively). Thus, given that most of
the LPEEs last for several precession cycles, they cannot be said to be simply times of maximum
seasonal contrast.
The authors also argue in lines 396-397 that maximum seasonal contrast at eccentricity maxima
produces dry conditions/reduced seasonal precipitation, although they have argued the opposite in
lines 370-385 (maximum seasonal contrast = wetter conditions/increased seasonal precipitation,
consistent with Reviewer 1 and, e.g., Bosmans et al., 2015). This identification of eccentricity maxima
with enhanced seasonal contrast is repeated in lines 410-411. If high seasonal contrast is considered
to produce overall wetter conditions due to enhanced seasonal and monsoonal precipitation and
increased extreme precipitation events, as argued in lines 370-385, then periods of maximum
eccentricity should be characterised by both enhanced dry (maximum precession/minimum seasonal
contrast/minimum seasonal precipitation) and enhanced wet (minimum precipitation/maximum seasonal
contrast/maximum seasonal precipitation) conditions. I could see an argument where the
haematite precursors are produced during the wet periods and then the haematite itself is produced
and transported during the dry periods, and thus the enhancement of both types of climate during
eccentricity maxima and LPEEs results in overall increased average haematite in the sediments. I
could also see an argument where the increased temperatures during LPEEs enhance the increase in
haematite formation and transport at times of minimum seasonal contrast (and therefore minimum
seasonal precipitation), which would also occur at times of maximum eccentricity. However, at
present, the argument about how eccentricity modulation of precession produces the observed
haematite variations is not clear to me.

Reviewer #3 (Remarks to the Author):

The authors have done a nice job revising the staging of the manuscript and interpretation of the
eccentricity signal in their records. One last suggestion, the authors probably would want to consider
removing or rewriting sentences/wordings related to the long-lasting effect of anthropogenic CO2
emissions (lines 33 to 34, 37 to 38). More recent studies generally agree that once 0 emission is
reached, CO2 level in the atmosphere will fall, and global warming will stop (e.g., Matthews and
Weaver 2010, Nat. Geo). This is due to the net absorption of CO2 by the ocean and land. These
statements can be considered as erroneous in the eyes of researchers who study modern climate.
